_export_meta.target_lesson_title: Promoting Health & Well-being — Role, Purpose & Supporting Individuals
_export_meta.adaptation_notes: BTEC Tech Award treats health promotion as part of the 'designing a health and wellbeing plan' workflow — the focus is the individual's plan rather than the role/purpose framework. This spec asks for a three-part framework (role/purpose/benefits) plus three named strategies (campaigns, education, strengths-based) which is examined as recall content. Build fresh from spec; use BTEC's plan-writing examples only as illustrative scenarios. The 'reduce health and social care costs' angle (benefit to the system, not just the individual) is unique to this qualification.

source_lesson.title: Lifestyle Indicators & Guidelines
source_lesson.description: The Eatwell Guide, CMO guidelines for activity, smoking, alcohol, and substance misuse.
source_lesson.content_html:
What Are Lifestyle Indicators?

While physiological indicators measure physical data like heart rate and blood pressure, lifestyle indicators focus on what a person does — their daily choices and behaviours. Health professionals use published guidelines to compare an individual’s lifestyle against recommended standards. The Component 3 specification requires you to know five areas of lifestyle indicators and their associated guidelines.

Lifestyle indicators are important because they reveal the causes behind abnormal physiological readings. If someone has high blood pressure and a high BMI, lifestyle indicators help identify why — perhaps they eat too much salt, do not exercise, and drink excessively. This makes it possible to recommend specific, targeted actions for improvement.

Nutrition — The Eatwell Guide

The Eatwell Guide is the UK government’s visual guide to a healthy, balanced diet. It divides food into five groups and shows the proportions in which they should be eaten.

Fruit and vegetables: Should make up just over a third of the diet. At least 5 portions a day. Provide vitamins, minerals, and fibre.

Starchy carbohydrates: Should make up just over a third of the diet. Includes bread, rice, pasta, and potatoes. Choose wholegrain varieties where possible for more fibre.

Proteins: Includes beans, pulses, fish, eggs, and meat. Aim for two portions of fish per week, one of which should be oily (e.g. salmon, mackerel). Choose lean cuts of meat and eat less processed meat.

Dairy and alternatives: Includes milk, cheese, and yoghurt. Choose lower-fat and lower-sugar options. Provides calcium for strong bones.

Oils and spreads: Needed in small amounts. Choose unsaturated oils (e.g. olive oil, rapeseed oil) rather than saturated fats (e.g. butter, lard).

Key Fact

The Eatwell Guide recommends: at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables per day, plenty of starchy carbohydrates (preferably wholegrain), some protein and dairy, and small amounts of unsaturated oils. It also advises drinking 6 to 8 glasses of fluid per day and limiting foods high in fat, salt, and sugar.

A health professional would compare an individual’s actual diet against the Eatwell Guide to identify areas for improvement. If someone eats very few vegetables, consumes too many sugary drinks, and regularly eats processed foods high in salt, these lifestyle choices increase their risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, CVD, and nutrient deficiencies.

Physical Activity — UK CMO Guidelines

The UK Chief Medical Officers’ (CMO) Physical Activity Guidelines set out the recommended levels of exercise for different age groups.

Children and young people (5–18 years): At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity every day, including activities that strengthen muscles and bones at least 3 days per week. They should also minimise the amount of time spent being sedentary (sitting for extended periods).

Adults (19–64 years): At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity (e.g. running, swimming). Additionally, adults should do strength-building activities on at least 2 days per week and reduce extended sitting time.

Older adults (65+ years): Same targets as adults, with added emphasis on activities that improve balance and coordination to reduce the risk of falls.

If an individual is not meeting these guidelines, they are at increased risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, depression, and some cancers. A health professional would assess the person’s current activity levels and recommend realistic ways to increase them.

Smoking — UK CMO Guidelines

The UK CMO’s position on smoking is clear: there is no safe level of smoking. The guidelines recommend complete abstinence — not smoking at all is the only way to avoid the health risks. Even light or occasional smoking increases the risk of lung cancer, heart disease, stroke, and COPD.

Key Fact

The CMO guideline for smoking is that there is no safe level. The only recommendation is to not smoke. For those who currently smoke, the recommendation is to quit completely using available support services such as NHS Smokefree.

Health professionals assess whether an individual smokes, how many cigarettes per day, and for how long. This data helps calculate the level of risk and the urgency of quitting. Support options include nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), prescription medications, counselling, and the NHS Smokefree helpline.

Alcohol — UK CMO Guidelines

The UK CMO Alcohol Guidelines recommend that both men and women should drink no more than 14 units of alcohol per week. These units should be spread over at least 3 days, with several alcohol-free days each week. There is no “safe” level of drinking, but staying within 14 units keeps the health risks low.

One unit of alcohol equals 10ml of pure alcohol. Examples: a single pub measure of spirits (25ml at 40%) = 1 unit; a small glass of wine (125ml at 12%) = 1.5 units; a pint of lower-strength beer (3.6%) = 2 units; a pint of higher-strength beer (5.2%) = 3 units. Many people underestimate how many units they consume because drink sizes and strengths vary. Binge drinking (consuming a large amount in a single session) is particularly harmful, even if the weekly total stays under 14 units.

Exceeding the alcohol guidelines increases the risk of liver disease, heart disease, stroke, some cancers (particularly mouth, throat, and liver), and mental health problems including depression and anxiety. A health professional would assess an individual’s weekly alcohol consumption and compare it against the 14-unit guideline to determine risk level.

Substance Misuse

For substance misuse, there are no “safe level” guidelines because the use of illegal substances like cannabis and opiates carries inherent health and legal risks. Health professionals assess whether an individual uses any substances, the type and frequency of use, and whether there are signs of dependency or addiction.

Key indicators of substance misuse problems include: using substances more frequently or in larger amounts over time, being unable to stop despite wanting to, neglecting responsibilities (work, family, education), needing more of the substance to achieve the same effect (tolerance), and experiencing withdrawal symptoms when not using. If substance misuse is identified, the individual may be referred to specialist services including drug and alcohol support teams, counselling, and rehabilitation programmes.

Lifestyle indicators work alongside physiological indicators to build a complete picture of a person’s health. For example, if an individual has high blood pressure (physiological) and the lifestyle assessment reveals they eat a high-salt diet, drink 25 units of alcohol per week, and do no exercise (lifestyle), the health professional can recommend specific, targeted changes — reduce salt, cut alcohol to 14 units, start gentle exercise. This is far more useful than simply telling the person their blood pressure is too high.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: In the exam, you may be given lifestyle data for a case study individual (e.g. “drinks 20 units of alcohol per week”, “exercises once a month”, “smokes 10 cigarettes per day”). Always compare the data against the published guideline and state whether the individual is meeting or exceeding the recommended levels. Then explain the health risks and suggest specific improvements. Using the correct guideline figures (14 units, 150 minutes, no safe level of smoking) shows the examiner you know the specification content.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lifestyle indicators assess an individual’s daily choices (diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol, substance use) against published guidelines to identify health risks.
  • Key guidelines: Eatwell Guide (balanced diet, 5 portions fruit and veg), CMO Physical Activity (150 min/week for adults, 60 min/day for young people), no safe level of smoking, and no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.
  • Lifestyle and physiological indicators work together — lifestyle data reveals the causes behind abnormal physiological readings, enabling targeted recommendations.

practice_questions.text: Identify one guideline used to assess an individual's nutrition.
Give two recommendations from the UK CMO Physical Activity Guidelines for adults aged 19-64.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct recommendation (max 2):
• At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week (1)
• Or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity per week (1)
• Strength-building activities on at least 2 days per week (1)
• Reduce extended periods of sitting/sedentary time (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a health professional could use lifestyle indicators alongside physiological indicators to assess an individual's health.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed explanation:
• Physiological indicators such as blood pressure and BMI measure the individual's current physical health (1). Lifestyle indicators reveal the behaviours that may be causing any abnormal readings (1).
• For example, if a person has a high BMI, lifestyle assessment may reveal they eat a poor diet and do little exercise (1). This allows the health professional to recommend specific changes such as following the Eatwell Guide and increasing physical activity to 150 minutes per week (1).
• Accept other valid examples showing how both types work together.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of the UK CMO alcohol guidelines in helping individuals maintain good health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion of guidelines and their importance with developed points.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points.
Indicative content:
• Guidelines recommend no more than 14 units per week for both men and women
• Units should be spread over at least 3 days with alcohol-free days
• Helps individuals understand their risk level — many underestimate consumption
• Exceeding guidelines increases risk of liver disease, heart disease, stroke, cancers
• Binge drinking is particularly harmful even if weekly total is within guidelines
• Guidelines give health professionals a benchmark to assess individuals against
• However, some individuals may ignore guidelines or not know about them
• Cultural and social pressures may make it difficult to follow guidelines.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which the Eatwell Guide is useful for improving an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Strengths of the Eatwell Guide:
• Visual and easy to understand — shows proportions clearly
• Government-backed, evidence-based advice
• Covers all food groups so provides comprehensive guidance
• Recommends specific targets (5 portions fruit/veg, 6-8 glasses fluid)
• Useful benchmark for health professionals to assess diet
Limitations:
• Does not account for individual needs (e.g. allergies, cultural/religious dietary requirements)
• Does not consider portion sizes or calorie needs for different people
• Some people cannot afford to follow it — fresh fruit/veg can be expensive
• Knowing the guidelines does not mean people will follow them
• Does not address eating disorders or emotional relationship with food
Conclusion: The Eatwell Guide is a useful starting point for nutrition advice, but it needs to be adapted to individual circumstances using a person-centred approach. It works best when combined with personalised support and when barriers such as cost, access, and knowledge are addressed.

practice_questions.text: Darren is 42 years old. A lifestyle assessment reveals that he eats takeaways 5 nights a week and rarely eats fruit or vegetables. He does no exercise and drives to work. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and drinks around 25 units of alcohol per week. His physiological indicators show a BMI of 34 and blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg. Using the case study, assess how Darren's lifestyle indicators compare to published guidelines and explain the risks to his health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive response comparing each lifestyle indicator against guidelines, identifying specific risks, and linking lifestyle to physiological data.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good comparison of lifestyle against guidelines with some risk analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparison but limited development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to guidelines.
Indicative content:
• Nutrition: Eating takeaways 5 nights a week and rarely eating fruit/veg is far below the Eatwell Guide recommendation of 5 portions a day and a balanced diet. High salt, fat, and sugar intake increases risk of obesity (his BMI is already 34 — obese), CVD, and type 2 diabetes.
• Physical activity: No exercise and driving to work means he is well below the CMO guideline of 150 minutes moderate activity per week. Sedentary lifestyle contributes to his obesity and high blood pressure. Lack of exercise also affects mental health — no endorphin release.
• Smoking: 15 cigarettes a day — CMO guidelines state there is no safe level of smoking. He is at increased risk of lung cancer, COPD, heart disease, and stroke. Smoking also raises blood pressure (his is already 150/95).
• Alcohol: 25 units per week is nearly double the CMO guideline of 14 units. Increases risk of liver disease, heart disease, cancers, and depression. Combined with smoking and poor diet, the risks are compounded.
• Links to physiological data: His BMI of 34 (obese) and blood pressure of 150/95 (high) are directly linked to his poor lifestyle choices. If he follows the guidelines, both could improve significantly.
• Overall: Darren is exceeding or failing to meet every guideline. The combination of multiple unhealthy lifestyle factors creates a compound effect, significantly increasing his short-term and long-term health risks. A person-centred approach would prioritise the most urgent changes while considering his preferences and circumstances.

glossary_terms.definition: Information about an individual’s day-to-day health behaviours such as diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol consumption, and substance use, used to assess how lifestyle choices affect their health.
A UK government guide showing the proportions of different food groups needed for a healthy, balanced diet.
A treatment that delivers small amounts of nicotine to the body to help reduce withdrawal symptoms and cravings when quitting smoking.
The harmful use of substances such as illegal drugs or the misuse of prescription medication, which carries health, legal, and social risks.
